blocks.text: Mark’s account names particular leaders, witnesses, officers, and a council in the proceedings against Jesus. It must not be read as blaming Jewish people collectively, or as authorizing antisemitism, claims of collective Jewish guilt, or caricatures of Judaism and its leaders.

The chapter gives agency to more than one group: an unnamed woman acts memorably in Bethany, Judas initiates betrayal, and arresting parties, priestly leaders, witnesses, and the council all take part in the developing conflict. This prevents the account from being reduced to the actions of a single person or group.

The narrative also places the disciples’ confident promises beside their flight at Jesus’ arrest. Within Mark’s larger portrayal of disciples who are called and authorized yet repeatedly fail to understand and protect themselves, their absence here makes following Jesus appear both as a gift and as a warning.

sections.title: People and Roles in the Narrative

blocks.text: Mark distinguishes the high priest from chief priests, elders, scribes, officers, and the council. These titles should not be treated as interchangeable names for one office; the account depicts several distinct roles within the hearing.

Jesus’ prayer preserves the Aramaic address “Abba” alongside the Greek “Father.” Elsewhere the same paired address appears in prayer. It conveys filial intimacy and dependence, but the word itself does not simply mean “Daddy,” nor does this prayer authorize unsafe submission to a human parent or authority.
